en: Salutations to Śrī Gāndharvikā and Giridhara, whose conduct is like that of pearls; who are more beautiful than ten million Cupids and possess the luster of a blooming blue lotus.
Salutations to the son of the Lord of Gopas, whose pastimes enchant the world.
I bow to the pair of Rādhā and Mādhava, who, in the year of the sport of buying and selling, have immersed their very selves in pearls while seeking victory over one another.
I worship Him who has arisen as the full moon in the sky of Śacī’s womb, in order to bestow upon the earth the nectar of His own radiant devotion.
In this place, [I behold] the one whose name is supreme, the Manu, as well as the son of Śacī;
here is the true form, Śrī Rūpa, his elder brother, the great city of Mathurā, the cowherd settlement, Rādhā-kuṇḍa, the preeminent mountain, and oh, the hope of Rādhikā and Mādhava!
I bow to that illustrious Guru, by whose renowned compassion [this state] has been attained.
We offer this wave of the nectar of Hari’s deeds, which has become an ocean of the waters of the Vṛndāvana forest,
full of aesthetic relish for the supreme bliss of the hosts of gods.
Once, Satyabhāmā, who had previously heard only a little of this history, asked Kṛṣṇa with a meaningful look:
"O blessed refuge, O Lord, where do those sweet vines grow,
whose fruit is the pearl set upon my bracelet?"
[* This verse is cited in UN 11.66 as an illustration of *maugdhya* (simplicity). In that context, the first line reads:
"What are those creepers? Where do they exist? Or by whom, indeed, were they planted?"*]
Then, remembering that incident, Kṛṣṇa, with a sense of inner weariness, laughed aloud and said:
"That time has passed when the birth of pearls occurred in creepers;
now, the causes for their production are the shells of oysters."
Then, having heard that unprecedented account, Kṛṣṇa was again entreated with a firm "So be it" by her, who was filled with an extraordinary longing to hear more; he spoke once more:
"Once, in the month of Kārttika, on Mount Govardhana in Gokula..."
There was a great festival of the Dīpamālikā;
therein, every person became supremely intent upon the preparation and accomplishment of various types of elaborate attire and requisites.
The cowherd men, moreover, while especially adorning themselves, were intent on decorating the cows and other livestock;
so it is said of the cowherd women.

Having adorned their dwellings, they became intent on preparing various ornaments for the sake of beautifying themselves. Rādhā, however, together with her circle of friends, was in the four-pillared pavilion of the mādhavī vine at the edge of the lake known as Mālyaharaṇa, fashioning various ornaments from the finest pearls.

He began [the narration]. And I, having heard that from the mouth of the young parrot named Vicakṣaṇa— whose name was truly significant— went there with curiosity to see that pair of cows, named Haṃsī and Hariṇī, who were the objects of his greatest affection.
Out of a desire for ornaments, pearls were requested from them. Then,
with the corner of her left eye— half-closed like the petal of a blue lotus and fragrant with the scent of manifold cleverness—
she glanced at me for just a moment as if with indifference.

To them— who, by means of a particular intensity of ecstatic immersion, were displaying the very play of stringing together necklaces and other ornaments, while their priceless great diamonds of laughter remained sealed by the lacquer of the sage’s vow— I addressed these words with a smile:
Their ears are veiled by the great mountain of towering pride, increased by the acquisition of the wish-fulfilling jewel of fresh youth;
[yet] at the request of me, their dear friend, they will for a moment lend their ears.
"May you ladies open it.
Then, among those who were looking at one another with slight smiles, the bold Lalitā laughed and spoke as if with indignation:
O noble citizen,
these pearls are of great value and are worthy of the king's queen.
"Truly, how could we not give these beautiful things for the very adornment of your queens?
Then, having heard those words, I, overcome with curiosity, spoke this very thing again and again in a conciliatory manner.
O dear ornaments!
If nothing at all may be given, then at least let that which is sufficient for the horns of my two most beloved cows be certainly given.
Then Lalitā, repeatedly shaking the pearls of them all, spoke again: "O Kṛṣṇa!
What should be done?
Not even a single thing suitable for your cow is here."
Then I said:
"O most clever Lalitā!
Wait, wait!"

Having reproached him, saying, "I am possessed by wretchedness; you will not be able to speak [thus] to me later," he quickly went to his mother, the mistress of Vraja, and said, "O Mother, give me pearls."
"But I shall sow them in the very furrowed field," I said again and again;
thereupon my mother laughed and said:
"My child, pearls do not grow from what is sown.
Then I said:
"Mother, let them certainly be given; they must be made manifest within three days at the latest," she said, and out of an inability to resist my persistence, she gave me many pearls.

Having constructed a small irrigation trench (*kedarikā*) three *puruṣas* deep at the bank of the Yamunā near the water-drawing ghāṭ of Gokula, I sowed seeds there and filled it again while some cowherd girls looked on with laughter.
A dense enclosure was constructed all around with wooden planks;
then, for the purpose of irrigating the small fields, a gate was opened so as to silence the sound of their voices as they uttered prayers for pearls.
When the cows were being requested [for milk], they laughed mockingly and said:
"How is it fitting for us to water that field of pearls with cow-milk,
since it was for the sake of adorning our beloved?"
"Let the watering of those pearl-fields be done with the milk of those very cows;
we must not harbor any desire for the fruit produced from those fields.
Having heard this, I—
By showing those cows of my own household, which had abundant milk, he performed the sprinkling every day;
consequently, on the very fourth day, pearls were produced.
Seeing this, I was filled with joy.
Taking his mother by the hem of her garment, he brought her and showed her those sprouts;
seeing them, however, his mother, wondering in her mind "What is this? and being filled with doubt, went toward Vraja.
Upon hearing this, the cowherd women said to one another with laughter, "The creepers have indeed grown into predators!
Then, before long, they observed that those pearl-creepers, which had previously bent their heads low, were now spreading out wide.
Descending gradually from above the nearby *kadamba* trees, they then,
within a few days, spread a sense of wonder among the cowherd girls with their clusters of flowers that maddened the bees with their fragrance, eventually taking possession of the entire Gokula.
Then, seeing those pearls born from them, which possessed a splendor distinct from the eight types of pearls produced from other sources, the inhabitants of Vraja were filled with great wonder,
especially the gopīs.
Then, having developed a longing through seeing him every single day, they consulted one another:
"O friends, we have learned from Bhadra that Kṛṣṇa will certainly not give us pearls at all.
Very well; it must not be that we have never seen the process of pearl cultivation performed by him."

Hearing the thought, "Why do they not abandon their lack of resolve there and begin work on that field twice as large?", the very clever Lalitā said: "O cowherd girls, you who are occupied with the wind-disease!"
The lifting of Govardhana Hill, the production of pearls from the earth, and other such deeds are tasks difficult even for those who have transcended the world;

therefore, it was certainly concluded by all the people of Vraja that whatever is performed with such ease must indeed be due to the power of great siddhis, such as medicinal herbs and mantras obtained through the Great Siddhas.

Otherwise, even though you know that such immense power could not have arisen spontaneously in that cowherd— who is but a tender blue lotus born from the lake of the womb of the wife of our Vraja-lord, and who knows only the entire range of his own cowherd birth, occupations, and arts— how could he possess it? Yet you [still] [act thus].

"Whatever they desire to undertake in such actions without the aid of perfected elixirs, mantras, and the like—that indeed leads only to their own drowning within the ocean of profound shame and ridicule upon its maturation; let this be understood as the truth.
Thereupon, Tuṅgavidyā said: "By us as well..."
"Having received a single perfected mantra from the presence of Nāndīmukhī, a disciple of the perfected mantra of the lotus feet of the venerable Bhagavatī, why is such an effort not made?
All of them, concluding that Tuṅgavidyā was speaking auspiciously, approached her side with humility.
They announced their desire for the Self.

Then Nāndīmukhī said to herself: "Ah! At long last, for the sake of making my own pair of eyes fruitful, [I shall behold] this wish-fulfilling tree of the sport of buying, selling, and play, which has been long desired by those like us."
"Indeed, by virtue of an extraordinary stroke of fortune for our eyes, this opportunity in the form of the Seed itself has suddenly presented itself before us;
and these women, too, are the crest-jewels among the wise."
Thinking, "I shall urge him toward this task by means of the excellence of my reasoning,
so that the tree may quickly become fully grown and bear fruit," she spoke the *nāndī* with inner joy: "O!"
Friends, it is true that this creation of pearls from clay was not produced by the power of Mantra Mukunda’s spells.

[The friends ask: "How is it that all these are perceived as being produced from clay—an impossibility—without the presence of their own source, such as the mother-of-pearl shell which serves as the cause?"

Nāndī: It is precisely because of the natural power of this earth that the ground of Vraja-forest—this mother of various jewels—is repeatedly extolled by the lotus feet of the Blessed Lord; for it is indeed the truth.

They are experienced in that very way; for here, golden trees are clearly seen born and being born, possessing coral, fresh sprouts, emerald leaves, clusters of diamonds and pearls, buds, lotuses, red fruit, and various other fruits.
They are seen; therefore, what is surprising that pearls sown in this [earth] will be produced and will bear fruit?

Thus, you too should perform that cultivation with great effort, preceded by the sprinkling of highly fragrant fresh butter and other substances, so that even more abundant and most excellent fruits may be obtained from it.

Thus, drinking in the sweetness of her words with satisfaction and praise, they all believed her; embracing her and returning to their own place, they summoned laborers by offering double or triple the milk products for their wages— compared to the standard rates— in competition with one another, establishing small fields in various locations for the purpose of cultivation.

Having placed in a casket all the loose ornaments as well as those that were fastened to the body, he preserved only a few as required; and having extracted the pearls from his person without exception, he sowed them daily at the three junctions of the day with cow’s milk, fresh butter, and fragrant ghee.
Thus they began to perform the consecration. Then,
upon hearing that pearls were being used for the ritual, out of envy and greed, Candrāvalī and all the other favorites—
even those who were more highly esteemed than her— placed [pearls] in various locations.
Having sown all their pearls without sparing even one from their bodies or their homes,
those beloved wives— after a few days, seeing the sprouts of predatory creepers grown in their respective fields and concealing their pride within— deceitfully [addressed] my dear friends.
They were mocked.
One day, observing an excessive expenditure of dairy products and the depletion of their respective households' supplies, the cowherds asked the cause with great agitation.
Having heard that, the elders said:
"O long-lived ones,
this is not a subject for inquiry by us, who are but children."
A great expenditure has been made for the sake of the pearl-fields; before long, a much greater profit will arise,
since it is said that even for the wives of kings, pearls are difficult to obtain from the black fields.
"They have been seen.
Then, on one occasion, Viśākhā, having observed those sprouts in her own garden plots, whispered this into the ear of one of them:
"O friends!
Such sprouts as were seen by me in the midst of the black field are not seen here."
"I do not know what will happen afterwards;
let them wrap themselves well under some pretext in order to ward off the glances of Kṛṣṇa’s companions.
Then, after a few days, by means of marks such as thorns on the fields of Rādhā and the other girls, as well as others...

When her own form was revealed by the creepers, it became renowned throughout all of Gokula that the predatory creeper had become a cowherd girl among the maidens. Having heard this, I reported it with a touch of irony at a musical gathering through the mediation of a friend.
"You have heard that many pearl-berries have grown in the fields. Since I am affectionate, let the first fruits be given to me along with my companions.
Then they said:
If we had practiced agriculture, then the entire cow-pen would have become composed of pearls;
having abandoned his own duty of cattle-rearing, who indeed is he?
One should resort to the livelihood of a plowman [in the alternative sense, the wretchedness of a beggar].
Having heard that, I [adorned] all my companions, cows with their calves, oxen that pull carts, buffaloes, goats with their kids,
and those dwelling in Vṛndāvana, with ornaments such as garlands made of pearls.

They were adorned; then the cowherd women, out of shame at being separated from their own ornaments, fearing the loss of much wealth, and out of dread of the cowherds, began to deliberate, "What is appropriate here?"

"Alas! We have been deceived by this wicked Nāndīmukhī, who has taken the dark side," she said; then, approaching the serpent in its presence, Nāndīmukhī was severely rebuked by them many times after they recounted what had happened, whereupon she replied: "O sirs!"
I swear by my ascetic powers that you have not been deceived by me in any way;
rather, all of this has been destroyed by you yourselves.

All: O deceitful one, how can this be? Nāndī: Because you haughty women, with a clamorous display like the beating of a *ḍhakkā* drum, made yourselves perfectly audible within the hollows of his ears as he was with his circle of companions, and then released [the arrows] into the fields.
Clearly, although they were sown, not even a single guard was stationed there.
All: What has not been accomplished by this much?
Nāndī (angrily): [What has not been accomplished?]
Listen to what has happened through those who consider themselves clever:
our city’s rogue teacher, having thoroughly enticed you with the gift of desired food, intended to defeat you.

Urged by him, the greedy Madhumangala, being excessively importuned, searched everywhere and gathered all the plants that had sprouted, leaving none behind; having planted them here and there among thickets of poisonous creepers, he then transplanted them individually into a single field of his own making where they had been sown from of old.
"In the same way, others were likewise brought and cast into the depths of the deep waters of the Kālindī; this I know with absolute certainty.
Having heard this, they all said, "O friend!"

O you whose sole purpose is to manifest the performance of the drama of deception, O you of blameless great bliss! O great holy field, which is like the preceptor Madhumaṅgala the jester! O you who are fit for the dance together with the rogue actor renowned in Vraja!
"O actress, most dear to him! O wretched Kali-yuga!
Stay, stay!"—having thus rebuked her with a frown of his brows, he returned to his own home.

Reflecting on that very same thing again and again, Rādhā said to her friends: "O friends, let Nāndīmukhī deceive him, or let that rogue do as he pleases; what is the use of considering that now? At present, no other sorrow is taken into account."
The very fear we have toward our teachers and others distresses us;
therefore, when pearls are shown to them, we would simply become slack.
Such things are altogether very difficult to obtain here; however, they should be acquired from Kṛṣṇa himself at a price.
In that regard, the means is as follows:
"Let it be considered. Then, after all had reflected, they said,
"Candramukhī is clever."
"Take gold and go; bring back pearls at their proper price. Then she said:
"I am unable to go alone into the presence of him who has now been reproached by us;
let Kāñcanalatā come along with me."
Thus, with the consent of all, they took much gold and approached the vicinity of the pearl garden;
there they spoke to Subala, the superintendent of that garden, who was seated together with me.
"O Subala,
we have heard that you are selling newly produced pearls;
therefore, here are these pure gold pieces."
"Having taken them, let the most exquisite pearls be given for their appropriate price.
Then, smiling, I said:
"At that time, though requested in many ways, not even a single pearl was [offered]."
"It was given to us!
And you did not give us a jar of milk for the purpose of watering our small fields. We should rather have thrown it into the middle of the Yamunā!"
Nevertheless, even if you were to stake the entirety of your household possessions as a wager, not even a single pearl extracted from the whole collection of pearls must by any means be given.
Then Kāñcanalatā said:
"If they did not fear their husbands and others for the sake of the pearl, who indeed could endure such a reproachful speech as this?"
"Let it be; what must be done?
Madhurā, with its many jewels spread out like a marketplace, is still far away. Therefore, my dear Subala, you yourself must act as a mediator today."
"We must also give a premium over the price of others. Then, upon hearing the word "premium," I said with a laugh,
"So be it."
But I, being naturally delicate like you, am unable to become hard; or rather, what else could be done without giving [the pearls]?
However, for all those who desire pearls—
"Will the determination of the pearl's value be made by you two alone?
They replied, "Of course. I asked, "What, then, is the distinction?"
Then Candramukhī, smiling slightly, looked toward Kāñcanalatā;
Kāñcanalatā then spoke to Subala with modesty.
Friend Subala, being yourself impartial, please compose yourself and accept this burden of well-deserved fame.
Subala said:
"Friend, how much of the great value of this secret is being revealed by the golden vine?"
"Why do you not accept it after clearly stating your own desired price yourself? To this, I replied:

"Friend Subala, the intention of Candramukhī has been understood; it was Kāñcanalatā herself who, considering pearls to be of priceless value, devised this plan and sent them through Rādhā and the others."
"They were given to me," he said;
"however, it is well known in the world that the value of pearls is greater than even that of a heap of gold."
Therefore, how could the value of these [other things] be fully met by a single golden vine?
Or rather, if there were many [such vines] in the form of two golden casket-like fruits upon her breast.
"Even though there are wish-fulfilling gems," the moon-faced one will say, "nevertheless, this is not so;
for even compared to the Kaustubha gem residing on the neck of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, this single pearl of mine is of supreme value."
Hearing that, Kāñcanalatā looked at me with a frown and said angrily: "O witless Candramukhī!
I told you right then and there that I would not [go] into the presence of that impudent man."
"You must go; nevertheless, you have troubled me by bringing this [fruit] with such persistence. You take these pearls and return; I am departing from here."
Candramukhī said: "Kāñcanalatā, you speak the truth; how then can the determination of the price be made by me alone?"
"How indeed can one remain here in solitude? For those who are designated as having a single yoga, there must be either joint engagement or joint withdrawal; therefore, I too must go.
Thus, both were prepared to depart.
Having seen this, I said: "Subala!
At that very moment, I said that no determination of the price would be reached by these two."
Having heard that, Subala approached them and said: "Friend Candramukhī,
a great insistence is seen on the part of my companion regarding the matter of the price."
Therefore, let my dear friend Rādhā come together with Lalitā and the others,
and right before our eyes, having paid the appropriate price, let her take the pearl ornaments she desires; in this matter,
I shall act as a mediator and provide assistance.
Having heard this, Candramukhī and Kāñcanalatā went into their presence and related everything that had occurred as if with indignation;
thereafter, Rādhā, together with Lalitā and the others, reached the edge of the pearl grove.
Candramukhī summoned Subala and said to him: "Dear friend Subala, you have boundless affection for us;
therefore, please arrange it yourself so that we may [be united]."
"Pearls are obtained at their proper price.
Having heard that, Subala informed me and, at my command, brought Lalitā and the others to my presence; however, regarding Rādhā, you [must inform her] of my arrival here.

Having addressed Subala, saying, "This must not be revealed in any way to my dear friend who has been troubling me," she remained hidden, listening to the entire account from within a Kadamba thicket situated near me.
Then, having observed them all, I asked, "How is it that Rādhā is not seen? To which Tuṅgavidyā replied:
"O Prince of Gokula, she has indeed been affectionately led away by the noble Jaṭilā to someone..."
A female guardian was present in the house for the sake of specific household duties;
then, Madhumangala, having entered at that very moment, perceived through gestures that Rādhā was standing nearby in secret, and having ascertained this, he smiled slightly.
I said: "Tuṅgavidyā, it appears that she has no desire to take the pearl. Thereupon, she replied: "No, no!"
"We ourselves shall pay the price for those pearls.
Then I said: "Viśākhā is indeed Rādhā, and Rādhā is indeed Viśākhā."
Therefore, it is understood that Viśākhā herself will pay its price;
let there be no insistence on that point.
But as for her who has come herself and does not take [the pearls], let four times their value be taken from her;
and the pearls shall be treated as common property.
"Let them be given," this was the firm resolve of all my friends. Thereupon, I said to Subala: "Friend Subala, [bring] caskets filled with gathered pearls."

"Bring them here, spread them out before me, and having sorted through them, take only the very finest pearls; disregarding even that former stinginess of yours, first offer them to Viśākhā for her sake, and receive their price from her."
Or, if he is unable to give what was proposed, then that must be disclosed:
let the cowherd girls who steal flowers and shoots be bound and guarded from afar right there at the Mādhavī bower where they are being protected.
Having heard that which was spoken by Madhumangala, [Kṛṣṇa said]: "Dear friend,
even in the face of confinement, the arts of escape have clearly been mastered by the wives of others."
Then I said: "Friend, this is indeed known to me as well;
however, there is no cause for concern, even though..."

For those such as us, touching another's wife and abandoning shame are utterly improper even in a dream; nevertheless— "A wise man should accomplish his own purpose, even while doing what is censured.
Likewise:
"Even in matters of food and worldly conduct, one should cast aside shame"—
by the force of this statement from the *Saṃhitā*, I myself shall become the watchman and dwell awake throughout the entire night without interruption.
Having heard this, Subala said with a smile: "O Puruṣottama,
how much longer must Viśākhā, my dear friend, remain in such great peril?"
Then I said: "As for the purpose for which this [woman] is being guarded, let her send the entire amount of the purchase price;
or else, having taken some small amount of goods herself, she will surely come here."

"Out of affection, having stayed here in this manner, he now sends her away for the purpose of bringing back the remaining goods; she must remain there for that time. Having heard this, Madhumangala said, "Friend!"

She is the mistress of these cow-pens, more expert than all others in every task, especially in running away with the cows; this has been witnessed by all of us again and again during the milking of the herd and other such occasions.
"But you toss about incessantly; from that, a great anxiety is known to me.
Then, turning aside with a smile, I said, "Friend!"
Enough with this anxiety; no agitation shall arise in me in his presence. Or, if it should arise, then [it will affect] my head.
Having made her lotus-stalk-like left arm a pillow,
and having placed my own reddish, sprout-like left hand upon the excellent bolster of the yellow silk garment shimmering upon her chest, in that manner...
I shall bring forth the playful eloquence of speech for the sake of a pearl-bet,
so that the four watches of the night may quickly come to an end while I remain awake in comfort; or else—
Having entered that prison cell within the dense darkness named my chest, which is so difficult to traverse,
and having firmly barred its two sides with the heavy bolts of my arms— the Garuḍa-birds—
I shall enjoy the pleasures of sleep at ease and without fear.
Having heard this, they all became smiling;
Rādhā, however, looking at me, Viśākhā, and all her friends with her neck uplifted, said: "O deer of Candrāvalī’s play!"
"Stay! Stay!
she said, threatening me without raising her voice, yet with a beautiful smile;
Viśākhā, however, was looking at me with a sidelong glance.
He said: "Go away, you shameless rogue! Speaking thus, she hid herself in the midst of her friends.
Then they all said to Subala: "Subala!"
Abandon your role as a jester;
if you have the desire to sell [it], [then do so].
"In that case, show us the pearls and let them be given to us at a fair price;
otherwise, we shall go home.
The pearls must be fetched from Mathurā itself."
Having heard this, Subala opened the caskets, showed me the pearls from them, and said to me:
"Dear friend, these pearls are priceless; with these, [one may obtain] a house, a wife, and so forth."

Even if one were to sell all the cattle together, it would be impossible to pay the price for even a single one; indeed, these cows, out of affection for you, disregard everyone else and know only you.
Therefore, this former display of wretchedness was [merely] for their sake.

"Even if you forget me, please consider that I am following you; therefore, having taken whatever small price is due, let the command be given to give these desired pearls as if they were given without price.
Then I said, "Friend!"
"No, no! We are engaged in the business of trade.
Let it be so. What?"
It must be done, and your word must be honored.
Therefore, let whatever small amount I seek be given only after it has been paid.
Furthermore,
it has been told to me by someone that you have repeatedly destroyed my offerings for the Ghaṭī festival by taking bribes;
therefore, the payment must be received by me from them in person.
Subala, smiling slightly, said: "Excellent words!
Moreover, having seen these [pearls] gathered individually by each [person] according to their own desired pearls and placed separately into small baskets."
"You too should state the price you desire.
Then I said, "Good sir, let each show his own desired pearls; the price shall be stated by me."
Subala said: "Dear friend, please consider with favor what these women have respectfully requested;
if it pleases you, then let it be done."
Then I said: "Subala, let it be told what they report; if it is appropriate, it should be done.
Subala replied: "They report as follows:"
Madhupurī is still far away,
and the collection of all the necessary goods and wealth must be accomplished within just two days; meanwhile,
the preceptor’s family is greatly distressed at every moment, as they have not yet seen even the ornaments of pearls and other such items.

He reviles us: "Having realized that those as affectionate as you have come into the depths of the lonely forest even casting aside shame, you must quickly depart after making us pay for pearls as if they were a mere debt."
"The purchase prices, together with the interest you desire, must be paid by us to you within two days; however,
if you do not have confidence in us, then you yourself must act as our guarantor."

Therefore, having gained confidence in these women— who are worthy recipients of the highest trust and who speak the truth consistently— one will soon obtain both the price for the pearls given and the desired profit;
it is the same with these [scriptures].
"Even though our affection is already deep, it will surely increase further.
Then, laughing, I said: "Subala, you are truly pure in intellect!"
Not even a slight portion of their conduct is known by you;
these women— a hunchback, a dancer, a Nāī, and a courtesan— having taken the pearl, [depart].

"If they remain playing, having entered their respective great mountain ranges— the families of their own gurus— which are surrounded by the great fortresses of their individual husbands, yet without giving up any of the wealth, what should you do? Subala said, "Friend!"
Do not speak thus;
these women will certainly not do so. Or, if they should do so, then you yourself must go there along with the Arjuna trees, cuckoos, and other creatures of the radiant forest, and [deal with] them.

It has been accepted. Having made my husbands hear that the price for these women consists of embracing, kissing, and drinking the nectar of their own lips, I shall demonstrate such fear to them so that they may obtain [the women] from me.
Just as they themselves will quickly dispatch those women to your presence and cause them to be given to you;
hearing that, Madhumangala said with anger: "O Subala!"
By name alone you are strong, O man;
in reality, however, you are seen repeatedly to have the form of a woman.
Since you even now desire to let out a hiss at these women’s husbands— who are more insignificant than the insignificant—
this is entirely appropriate for one of such timid nature as yourself.
Therefore, you yourself should sit here;
taking up the expedition led by Vijaya and others, you must forcibly surround and bring back their cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, along with their owners,
and having confined them, they shall be guarded here in the city of Nadīśvara.
Then, they themselves will come and, having given back their respective property most abundantly, will liberate each of their husbands as well as their cattle and wealth.
Thereupon, overwhelmed by the great burden of suffering born from hearing that news, I said: "O friend of my life!"
Madhumangala!
How can you speak in such a manner?
Even the Bhillas, Pulindas, and others who dwell in Vraja—
They are dearer to me even than my own beloveds;
moreover, these kinsmen and uterine brothers are truly non-different from me.
Therefore, this deliberation is utterly improper.
Only what was spoken by Subala appears somewhat plausible;
nevertheless, the preservation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) does not occur at all through the practice of taking and giving with those who are dear. And so says the *Smṛti*:
"For neither taking nor giving is extended among friends; when a favor is done out of affection, there may be a lapse, and immediately after that, a quarrel.
Therefore, let them take the pearls after paying only the price originally agreed upon.
Having heard that and observing Subala as if he were filled with anger, [he said]: "Ah!
O Subala, who has reached the further shore of the art of Kautilya!
We have been brought here by you all together solely for the purpose of being mocked. Therefore, you—"
"Rule the kingdom through the business of pearl trade;
we have set out," they said.
As they were departing, Subala approached them and, manifesting his friendship, spoke softly to Lalitā.

She said: "Friend Lalitā, because the practice of buying and selling causes the breaking of affection, my dear friend has proposed this determination of value out of fear of that alone, without any acquisition of the wealth currently offered."
"In every way pearls must not be given"— this has been determined in all respects.
Therefore, first come together and let the price alone be settled.
"Therefore, the means for that gift must be considered later";
with these conciliatory words, he turned them back, brought them to my presence, and said to me: "Friend, setting aside the joke, let the price be stated first."
Then I said: "Friend Subala,
first of all,
whose pearls should have their price told?"
Subala said: "Among these, Lalitā alone is the foremost; therefore, let the price of this pearl first be determined.
Then, smiling slightly, I said: "If, in battle, by her prowess, Lalitā—who is most skilled among those who carry such [pearls]—"
"A lion among men such as I can be rendered powerless even once;
therefore, in her presence,
I shall by no means remain weaponless."
Or rather, let her remain unmarried for life and follow this very man, constantly reciting his praises; let her take him by paying whatever price is required.
Subala smiled and said: "O hero of Gokula!
For seven nights here, with the weight of your intensely blazing pride, you shall serve to shatter the mountain of Mahendra’s arrogance."

How can this delicate and graceful girl, O fierce one, prolong the assembly with you, by whom Mount Govardhana was made to rest like a bee upon the tip of the cowrie-shell held on the little finger of your lotus-like left hand?
Madhumangala said: "Subala,
why do you so highly praise his former pride displayed during his childhood?"
"Now that he has been made to sprout with a hundred thousand times the qualities of the wish-fulfilling tree of Darpaka by the sprinkling of the nectar of youth," Subala said, "How is this known?"
Madhumangala: As for how he previously caused such distress to all his former enemies,
now he shall do the same to this fortress, which is as dear to his heart as a mountain is to his body.
And by whom, with mere sport, has he been cut into pieces by the weapon of his claws alone, and even from that state reduced to incomparably greater distress by Mahāmāra and others?
Then, laughing, I said: "Subala!"
It is true that elsewhere I appear as such; however,
not so in her presence, for she is repeatedly skilled in displaying various wonders even through this most excellent form.
"I have been rendered motionless with ease by the mere twang of her bow-like eyebrows, as if by the sound 'hum. So how can this woman remain powerless?"
Hearing this, Lalitā looked at her friends with smiling faces; then, suppressing the physical manifestations arising from her own joy, she spoke as if in anger: "O Subala, Vidūṣaka!
[You who are] accompanied by Madhumangala!"
"O Goddess Bhaṇḍatā of Gokula-bhaṇḍa, it is true that you have also possessed him!
For, having summoned us here in his presence, he casts us into an ocean of mockery; and saying 'Look at the spectacle!', he insults me with a crooked glance, crying out, 'Come here, O simple ones!'"

Having said, "Come," just as she was departing together with all of them, the venerable Paurṇamāsī’s female disciple Nāndīmukhī arrived there at that very moment and related the entire account of her departure to all of them.
Having reflected thus, she said: "Friend Lalitā!
Why do you depart, disregarding your own duty at the mere words of jest from this playful son of the illustrious King of Vraja?"
Having attained peace for a moment with me—
placing dishonor before you and casting pride behind you.
A wise person should accomplish his own task; for the ruin of one's duty is indeed folly.
Having endured such jests and mockeries according to this principle, maintain your steadfastness and accomplish your own purpose. Furthermore, I speak having made an oath;
by his very jokes, as if by sureties, [the matter is secured].
Pearls should be given;
otherwise, even though he remembers his former meanness, this proud man will find it impossible to engage in jesting.

"Having heard the price of that other pearl, one should deal in it only if it would be beneficial," she said, as if by force; and taking her by the hand, she brought her along with all the others to the vicinity of the pearl-vendor and spoke to me, O Prince of Gokula.
In this regard, your venerable lady has sent a certain message to you, preceded by hundreds of auspicious blessings;
therefore, O Nāndīmukhī, I—
Is it well with your ladyship, the Blessed One?
Please tell me, what are your commands?
"I nourish myself as well with the nectar of her message.
Nāndīmukhī said: "These young girls of Vraja, Rādhā and the others, are objects of our exceeding affection; they, too, O long-lived lady, are constantly and supremely devoted to you."
Therefore, seeing our excessive persistence,
please abandon it; instead, having taken their price as it can be afforded, you, the son of Vraja’s lord who possesses eight treasures, should give these desired pearls to them, and we—

"Having understood this message from the Blessed One— that they are to be gratified— please set aside jests and, by satisfying them with gifts of pearls, you, O noble ones who bring happiness to all of Gokula, are the sole authority to send them back home."
Then, with praise, I said: "O Nāndīmukhī!
Having previously placed upon my head that flower of the command sent by him through the hand of Subala, I have completely renounced everything, save for some of Lalitā’s pearls."
"The value [of this] has been determined along with her; having heard that from her own mouth, whatever you abandon, that too shall be abandoned by me.
Hearing this, Lalitā—her lips trembling and knitting her eyebrows—was joined by all the others, whose faces were lit with smiles.
Looking [at him], Nāndīmukhī said with a smile: "O Prince of the Vrajas!
He has indeed been heard of by these women, but such playful jesting was conducted by him in the absence of me and in the presence of all the others."
"Let the appropriate price be stated.
Then I said, "Nāndīmukhī, Jyeṣṭhā is the most excellent of all these; therefore, [the price] for her..."
"Having deliberated upon the value of this pearl together with her, you yourself must state it.
Nāndīmukhī replied, "The owner of the wealth himself must first state the value;
therefore, let him do so himself."
"Let that be told by you.

Then I said: "When Rādhā has risen in the celestial path of my heart, which belongs to the Lord of Night, and when Anurādhā is rising, Jyeṣṭhā rises between those two with passion, having cast aside her own boundaries."

"May he embrace my moon-like face with theirs, whether together or separately, even if only slightly. Then, having heard this, while Rādhā remained hidden within the bower and Lalitā, Viśākhā, and Jyeṣṭhā were there— these three— [Kṛṣṇa spoke].

As they were expressing their anger with a knitting of the brows, I said: "Nāndīmukhī! Having understood that what has been spoken brings great profit to each of you, why are these women angry? Nāndīmukhī replied: "O handsome one!"

For us— who are chaste wives belonging to another, and for whom this moon-like face of another man is like that of a stranger to the dark lord of the night at Gokula— let alone kissing his moon-like face, even the mere touch would lead only to great sin.
Having heard such playful jesting as "they are angry," and so forth, Satyabhāmā said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Lord!
In the counting of the stars..."

It is entirely appropriate that anger arose in both the clever Rādhā and Viśākhā— who, while each perceiving her own turn in the playful conversation, deliberately employed the name "Anurādhā" instead of the well-known names "Rādhā" and "Viśākhā"— for they were acting with intentional significance.
"How can Lalitā be angry? Kṛṣṇa said, "My dear,
'Anurādhā' is merely another name for Lalitā herself."
Satyabhāmā: O Lord of the Yādavas!
My mind finds no sufficient satisfaction from hearing these accounts of your unprecedented pastimes; therefore, speak, speak!

Kṛṣṇa: Then, beholding her moon-like face—variegated with a smile like a *campaka* creeper—and moving with my hand that heap of pearls she had grasped, I said this: "Nāndīmukhī! For many days I have thought that this dear friend of yours, Campakalatā, has obtained spiritual perfection from some *siddha*."
[He] remained reflecting.
Nāndīmukhī asked, "How was it inferred?
I replied, "Because this Campaka creeper, though stationary, is bent down by the weight of two large fruits in its center."
And as he wanders about with playful ease,
may the Campaka garland, having become one upon my chest which is as beautiful as a rain cloud, perfume me with the abundance of its own fragrance.
By the power of my own accomplishment and by her command alone, I must also quickly place upon her neck a very fine necklace of emeralds and between her breasts a central sapphire.
Subala: Dear friend, the attainment of this [state] through walking meditation and other such practices is indeed experienced by everyone;
yet for you, it has never been seen by anyone, at any time, or anywhere.
Therefore, if you, having suddenly set out upon this difficult task, should find it impossible to accomplish, we shall mock you for these [efforts].
Therefore, one must act only after having investigated.
Thus I said: "Subala, even though you see my accomplishment, do you not see it?"
"What must I do?
Nāndīmukhī said: "O Madhurāṅga, when, where, and what accomplishment has been achieved by you? That [must be told]."
"Let it be told; all are eager to hear.

Thereupon I said: "O King, during the festival procession in Ambikāvana, a great python, having fallen at my father's feet as one seeking refuge, was adorned with every ornament by the mere touch of my big toe."
I became the king of the Vidyādharas;
and Govardhana, the king of mountains, was held up by me for seven days with a single hand, as effortlessly as if it were a mushroom.
The group of companions, including Subala and others, who had been deluded by the flames of Kāliya’s poison,
were clearly restored to consciousness by his mere glance;
even the great forest fire was repeatedly turned into nectar and clearly consumed with ease— such are [his deeds].
"Who has not experienced many manifestations of supernatural power in Gokula?
Enough of this excessive detail.
Hearing this, Lalitā, smiling slightly, said: "Nāndīmukhī!"
This city-dweller of yours, though ill-behaved,
tells all this truthfully;
however, that time has passed.
Where all that had been accomplished through the power of his celibacy,
[now occurred] regarding the wife of the cruel Kaṃsa’s servant Govardhana-malla, Padmā, Śaivyā, and others.

Because my celibacy had been defiled by the continuous amorous dalliances with the women of Vraja, all those supernatural powers (siddhis) vanished from me. Then, laughing slightly, I said: "O Lalitā!"
Without having understood the meaning of this verse— "Just as fire, which consumes all things, incurs no fault for its intensity"—
you have said this; therefore, let the meaning of each [word] be heard, as follows:
Even by consuming everything, there would be no diminution of the fire's brilliance;
on the contrary, its increase becomes truly great.
So it is with excellent women such as yourselves.

Madhumangala: "O Lalitā! By the sweetness of the constant enjoyment of the flavor of uninterrupted passion, my own spiritual perfection (*siddhi*), becoming ever more radiant, has attained a state of supreme and even greater increase."
"Your dear friend speaks the truth:
if spiritual accomplishment does not lead to further progress, then how can one who is liberated ascend upon the earth?"
And how is it that the climbing vines, having ascended, spreading in every direction, blossom and bear fruit so abundantly?
Lalitā, smiling, said: "Noble Madhumangala!"
Is that the power of Siddhi, your dear friend?
Madhumaṅgala: Of whom is it?
Lalitā: [From the very land of Vṛndāvana. Rādhā (to herself): "O Lalitā, let it be said that this is the company of amorous women," thus was it spoken by Rādhā.
Viśākhā also spoke in response.
Then I said: "How is it that you yourselves have sown and released these very predatory creatures right here?
Lalitā replied: "O crest-jewel of the clever!"
"Do those who are liberated become harmful? I asked, "In that case, why are they not reborn? Lalitā replied, "Due to the deficiency of the specific soil and the seed."
Rādhā (to herself): O Lalitā!
Viśākhā also said that this should be told even because of the excellence of this sacred field.
Nāndīmukhī: Lalitā!
Viśākhā speaks the truth indeed.
Lalitā: How so?

Nāndīmukhī: Because in this Vṛndāvana— a great field exceedingly lush with the celestial creeper of nectar-like devotion, which is ignited by the weight of love that constantly bestows supreme bliss, and which is like a magnificent saline soil for the poisonous vine of liberation that always pervades every limb— any living beings who certainly come here are surely devotees alone.
"How indeed can they become liberated?
Lalitā laughed and said, "Viśākhā,
it is clear that even the playful charm of your speech is characterized by attachment to lovers."
It will be coherent; explain it by unfolding its meaning.

Viśākhā said: "By the maxim that even a yogi who has ascended to the heights is cast down by attachment to the lower realms, how much more so one of meager accomplishment—such as this person, whose body, mind, and lineage are exceedingly darkened, and who is a connoisseur of the flawed flute."

Though they were liberated by a mere moment of attachment, they again encountered birth through dwelling in a womb upon the earth; having become porous once more, they became bound by the qualities of saṃsāra.
Therefore, O Viśākhā—
"You speak nothing but the truth.
Subala said, "Friend, how so?
Then I replied, "The qualities of my teacher in the arts of love—his beauty, his skill, and so forth—"

Having heard in particular from the mouths of Nārada and others about those liberated while living who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, they were filled with wonder; then, having accepted birth in the houses of the foremost cowherds in this Gokula forest— a place crowded with rigorous austerities— they became the playful damsels of Vraja, enveloped by qualities such as exquisite essence and cleverness, just like these very women.
Just as flower garlands shine upon my chest,

so too do others— even those who have attained supreme liberation— being drawn by my inconceivable qualities, dwell eternally among the perfected beings here in this forest of Vraja, both stationary and moving.
Having become beasts, birds, trees, and so forth, they delight me by tasting supreme bliss;
thus they bring joy.
Subala: Friend!
"Well described!

Lalitā, smiling slightly, said: "If, O Great Siddha, by the power of your accomplishment pearls are produced even without the specific qualities of their respective strata, then you are indeed a Supreme Siddha."
"How have you come to engage in this petty trade of selling it for the sake of gaining even a mere trifle of wealth?
Then I said: "O foolish Lalitikā!
Just as you women, arrogant with youth and wealth..."

Just as one who abandons his own duty wanders aimlessly here and there, should I too— being the only son of the illustrious King of Vraja, the crest-jewel among Vaiśyas who was perfectly established in his own duty— abandon my own dharma and become unrestrained?
Since agriculture, commerce, cattle-rearing, and money-lending are said to be the fourfold [means of livelihood], we Vaiśyas have these four occupations;
by the practice of even one of these occupations alone—
For me, who practices that quartet which brings about the increase of all accomplishments, accomplishment has indeed reached its highest limit and shines forth supremely.
Nāndīmukhī, with a smile: O Crown Prince, you who are steadfast in your own duty! Regarding you...
Agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing—these three modes of livelihood are clearly experienced; however, living by usury has never been considered at all.
Therefore, O Nāndīmukhī, I say:
Even though that [activity] is being performed by us, why is it not perceived by you?

Even now, he has begun to establish an increase in the operation of the infinite liberated ones, having transferred his own nature to these [liberated souls] who are agitated by the absolute non-existence of liberation.
"I am here," said Viśākhā, smiling slightly, "Subala, wherever one finds delight."
Indeed, he extols even that which is censurable as being praiseworthy;
therefore, for the time being, there is an excellent description even of unrighteousness (*adharma*) as something beautiful.
"This is not improper for your dear friend.
Subala laughed and said, "Nāndīmukhī!
He gains not only an increase in wealth, but—"
Other entities as well are undergoing increase moment by moment.

Nāndīmukhī: Of whom? Of whom? Subala: First, of his fresh youth which surpasses ten million Cupids in every limb; of the rolling of his eyes at the corners of his gaze which mocks the trembling lotus; and of his speech, which possesses a sweetness as radiant as the essence of nectar.
Madhumangala: Subala!
Have you forgotten the increase in the value of other commodities?
Subala: Whose increase am I being reminded of?
Madhumangala:

[He is the source] of the sweet pastimes and amorous sports born of the pride of supreme beauty, manifested through his shark-shaped earrings, jeweled anklets, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, jeweled rings, and so forth.
Lalitā: Noble sir, how have you concealed the increase of one particular thing?
Nāndīmukhī: Of which one?
Lalitā: [It is the remains of the nectar from the lips] of the virtuous women of Ballava’s clan.
Rādhā (smiling): O Lalitā!
Truly, truly, her very form proclaims that this was indeed her meal.

By the very drinking of this most excellent elixir, his pair of arms attained a girth that crushes the pride of well-rounded sapphire bolts, and his chest a breadth that destroys the arrogance of emerald door-panels.
In her two thighs,
there was a perfect roundness that stripped away the pride of emerald plantain stalks; and in her face,
there was an intense loveliness that caused the sweetness of even the full autumnal moon to shrink away.
In his two feet, there was a sweetness that put to shame the praise of fresh mango sprouts;

in every limb, there was a charming elegance that caused even modesty to feel ashamed through its skillful and most sweet arrangement; and in his body, there was a weight of manifest brilliance spreading forth, captivating the luster of fresh clouds, blue lotuses, and sapphires.
Since that nectar of his gentle speech has shone forth, pervading every part of her being, it was further perfumed by Viśākhā with the blossoms of her own clear and sweet words spoken with a smile.
Madhumaṅgala, reflecting, said: "Friend!"

These cunning women, alluring you— who are greedy for the sweet lips of another's beloved— with an abundance of sweetness in their most delicious words, having promised a much greater increase of profit, take your pearls and resort to inaccessible places such as the matted locks [of ascetics].
Knowing well that they will not even give the principal, let alone any news of interest, I am informing you that I should be wished well by my friend for his own benefit.
"Whatever pleases you first, then I shall bite my tongue with my teeth— O friend!
These women here, such as the Gāndharvī and others, are ladies of noble family."
In matters of taking and giving according to one's desire, you are exceedingly pure; however, this was said by you quite unknowingly. Listen now:

having greatly delighted me by offering the nectar of your lower lip, you have, through the Gandharva rite, placed upon your own breast this pair of streaks from the red lac of my lotus-feet, which were taken by me this morning.
Having adorned my chest with that very [garment] folded fourfold, it was bestowed by Lalitā this very evening;
and on the evening of the day after tomorrow, she will take a single magnet-gem that distills nectar according to the Kali method.
Having purified it by multiplying it threefold,
Viśākhā also, at midnight, with great longing, took the nectar of my sweet lower lip— which was her very own essence— and in the morning, multiplied that very same thing many times over.
"Having given [it], I am indeed satisfied.
And Campakalatā and the others, repeatedly and insistently grasping their respective desired objects— some doubling them and some [others]— [presented them].
Having presented them tripled, they have exceedingly delighted me;
however, regarding these two women,
their disposition toward giving is somewhat different.
Nāndīmukhī: Which one is she?
Then I [replied]: One is Raṅgaṇavallī, who has consented to place upon my chest three pairs of her own perfectly round and sweet fruits.

Having taken two mango fruits from my hand, she offered them both at once; though they were indistinguishable, she did not perform the act of offering them twice, having already completed the action of going.
Another woman, a companion of Raṅgaṇamālā—
Having said she would give a bouquet for my exclusive embrace by doubling the number of *tulasī* flowers,
she now merely delays the time, saying "it should be given now" or "it should be given then," and does not even offer the roots.
Madhumangala: O Raṅgaṇavallī and Tulasī!
Although our dear friend Priyaṃvada has obtained divine substances from you both, he remains naturally simple by disposition.
One such as you speaks only what is pleasing;
nevertheless, even toward such a person as this, you two practice the art of deception, and out of ingratitude, you feel no fear of the ways of the world.

Hearing that, Lalitā laughed charmingly and said: "O noble Madhumangala, friend, for whom is your speech not dearer than nectar? In this assembly, every syllable and every word of yours is like a harsh thunderbolt to the liars; yet, alas, there is no great fragrance here!"
Then, amidst laughter and clamor,
saying "Well done, Lalitā!
Well described!", they all embraced her.
And Rādhā likewise thought in her mind:
"O Mohan, [you are] Nāndīmukhī!"
How is disbelief established?
This Raṅgaṇamālikā is a recipient of Lalitā’s love.
And Viśākhā, who is dear to her disciples, is the second; she will certainly cause him to give that away once she has awakened him through these two,
by means of your repeated pure devotion toward them both.
This legal procedure is carried out as follows:
if it is not possible to compel payment, then the remaining amount of that property is paid by the two themselves out of affection for him.
If even these two do not immediately agree to grant it,
then you cannot be questioned by anyone;
for as soon as you begin to hiss in the presence of Anaṅgamañjarī’s sisters, they themselves will [act].
Accompanied by an increase in her agitation, she will quickly and most certainly distribute it.
Then, while all the women, including Nāndīmukhī, look at me with the crookedness of a frown on their brows, Tuṅgavidyā approaches slightly and says with an inner smile: "O friends!"
"Listen to this unprecedented news.
All: "Friend, what is it?"
Tuṅgavidyā: A certain teacher named Kāntadarpa is heard of.
Lalitā: He is heard of by tradition, my lady, but he is not known [to me]. Tuṅgavidyā: By his dear disciple named Śyāmala Miśra, of the sūtras composed by him...
"Regarding the statement 'the fourfold junctions are explained as the functions of the *kṛt* suffixes'—are those four functions that have been explained actually observed in practice by you?
Viśākhā: "Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu! Let alone seeing those functions; he himself has never even appeared."
[He] has come within the range of hearing.
Lalitā, with a meaningful look, said: "Tuṅgavidyā!
Where was he known by you?"
Tuṅgavidyā— Sakhīsthalya had come here in the evening to search for him, in order to recover a single great lotus-apsaras from its stalk;
therefore, I said, "Tuṅgavidyā!"
"How can there be movement across such a vast distance?
"By the power of the abundant growth of lofty knowledge in the forest.
Hearing this, they all smiled.
They were doing so.
Lalitā: And then?
Tuṅgavidyā: First, by Śyāmala Miśra’s peerless rival, the royal scholar Alīka...
Having composed the *Narma-pañjikā* and the *Kraya-vikraya-pañjikā*, I have now elaborated upon the *Alīka-pañjikā* and likewise the *Tathādāna-pradāna-pañjikā*.
I believe that you ladies have heard this set of four *pañjikās* as they were successively elaborated under their respective names.
Lalitā: And what? Is he also being well-regarded?

Tuṅgavidyā: Even more than them, Kuhakabhaṭṭa—who is a fellow student of his and possesses the boldness of an exceptionally sound and sharp intellect—has begun to compose commentaries on all four of those works simultaneously.
Campakalatā: Tuṅgavidyā!
You are proficient in all branches of knowledge; therefore, they all desire to learn from you the names and etymologies of these four authors of the treatises.

Viśākhā: The meaning of "Ācārya-Bhaṭṭa" is indeed clear; let that of "Miśra-Paṇḍita" be explained. Tuṅgavidyā laughs and says: "He has both faults and virtues; because he is mixed [with both], he is called 'Miśra'."
Nāndīmukhī: Which is the fault, or which is the virtue?

Tuṅgavidyā: The fault is that, without discriminating between cleverness and lack of cleverness, one proceeds everywhere indiscriminately. [The virtue is] that, due to an abundance of simplicity, one acts everywhere without partiality, without even distinguishing between the superior and the inferior.
"Engaging with equanimity is a great virtue.
Lalitā smiled and said, "In that case, this path of mingling is indeed appropriate for him.
Citrā said, "Let the learned one also be told."
*Tuṅgavidyā* is the intellect (*buddhi*) that discriminates between the existent and the non-existent;

one endowed with that is a *paṇḍita*. However, by virtue of the weight of this [latter] intellect, having deliberated that "between the preceding and the following, the subsequent rule is stronger," the latter [intellect] is that which discriminates the non-existent.
That which is wisdom (paṇḍā), relying on that very thing as its superior state, one is called "wise" (paṇḍita) because of being endowed with it.
Citrā: Friend Tuṅgavidyā, let the meaning of even the fourfold [periods] beginning with twilight be explained after it has been illuminated.
Tuṅgavidyā— In this painting,
she alone is skilled in such elaboration within our circle; let her herself explain it.
Lalitā: I have never heard even a slight mention of this in the Citra;
however, Tuṅgavidyā, who is the commentator on this very section, surely knows its meaning.
Citrā: O Tuṅgavidyā!
You are bound by oath upon my head; you yourself must explain this.
Then, out of extreme bashfulness, she herself did not speak, [referring to] Rādhikā, who is the supreme object of affection and who has not been mentioned even slightly.
While Tuṅgavidyā was looking with a smile and a narrowing of her eyes at the young girl, the best of earthly dancers, who was the companion of his pleasure and known as Tuṅganarmā— the female jester—
Tuṅganarmā [said] something.

Having sat down and gazing at my face with a smile, she said: "O Citrā, that matter is not yet understood by us; however, after that celestial nymph had returned again and again and, with great humility and persistent insistence, won over the venerable Miśra—who possesses words of true meaning—we have studied it from him."

Listen as I briefly relate that commentary on the fourfold conduct (*vṛtti*) which was composed by me in the presence of Tuṅgavidya along with our companions, including all its auxiliary parts: first, hear that "union" (*sandhi*) is the meeting of the two young people, brought about either through a female messenger or by their own initiative.
Its function consists of the Vivaraṇa, Matisāra, and so forth;
from that [arise] the varieties of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), consisting of the touching of the breasts, embracing, kissing, and drinking from the lips.
The fourfold [set] is indeed the fourfold;
its respective occurrence consists of things such as nail-marks and so forth,
and arm-binding, neck-chains, and so forth.
On the cheeks, there was the playful placing of the lotus-face and so forth,
as well as bites and other acts performed with cleverness;
thereafter, their mutual joking conversation was related.
